paragraphs: A robot can understand what a cup is yet still fail to identify which cup belongs to a particular person. This paper studies personalized manipulation: selecting and handling a specific object that was unseen during training, using only a few reference images. The challenge is connecting a general instruction to the correct physical instance among similar objects.

Visual Attentive Prompting, or VAP, adds a perceptual adapter to an existing, frozen vision-language-action model. It stores reference images as visual memory, detects candidate objects in the scene, and compares their visual representations with those references. It then highlights the matched object and rewrites the instruction to direct the model’s attention. This personalization requires no additional model training.

The authors introduce two simulation benchmarks and a real-world tabletop benchmark spanning multiple robots and tasks. VAP consistently improves both task success and manipulation of the correct object compared with generic policies and token-learning baselines. The results support visual prompting as a practical way to translate object recognition into personalized robot actions.
icml-2026-bring-my-cup-personalizing-vis.tldr: VAP uses reference images and visual prompts to help frozen robot models manipulate the correct personal object without additional training.

paragraphs: Increasing a neural network’s size changes how its parameters and learned representations behave during training. Parameterization schemes aim to manage those changes so that larger models remain trainable and settings chosen for smaller models remain useful. Such benefits have been observed with fixed data distributions, but reinforcement learning introduces a complication: the agent’s actions change the data it subsequently learns from.

This paper empirically compares two scaling regimes for reinforcement learning agents. CompleteP represents a rich regime that maintains feature learning, while the Neural Tangent Kernel parameterization represents a lazy regime. The study examines whether hyperparameters transfer across model sizes, how consistent learned features and policies remain, and how learning behavior changes as agents grow.

Across multiple control tasks and variants, agents trained with CompleteP achieve better compute and reward efficiency than agents using the NTK parameterization. The finding supports preserving representation learning when scaling reinforcement learning systems. Its significance is empirical: parameter scaling choices influence how productively additional model capacity translates into learning and control performance.
icml-2026-completep-for-rl-maintaining-f.tldr: CompleteP improves compute and reward efficiency over NTK parameterization when scaling reinforcement learning agents across the studied control tasks.

paragraphs: Checking language-model answers often depends on other imperfect models, such as judges or reward models. Combining several verifiers could improve those judgments, but learning how to combine them usually benefits from known correct and incorrect answers. Obtaining those labels can be expensive, especially for difficult questions whose answers are hard to establish.

Fully Unsupervised Score Ensembling, or FUSE, combines verifiers without ground-truth correctness labels. Its central idea is to control conditional dependencies between the verifiers. These relationships matter because the usefulness of multiple judgments depends on how their information overlaps. FUSE manages those dependencies to improve the unsupervised performance of spectral ensembling algorithms.

In test-time scaling experiments spanning different answer-generating models, verifiers, and benchmarks, FUSE typically matches or improves upon semi-supervised alternatives. Evaluations include GPQA Diamond, Humanity’s Last Exam, and IMO Shortlist questions. These findings suggest that carefully handling relationships among imperfect verifiers can yield useful combined judgments even without labeled examples for fitting the ensemble.
icml-2026-fuse-ensembling-verifiers-with.tldr: FUSE combines imperfect verifiers without correctness labels and typically matches or exceeds semi-supervised alternatives in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting benefits from examining changes at several temporal resolutions. Different scales expose different patterns, but existing approaches commonly rely on fixed, discrete choices of scale. This paper organizes those approaches into a shared family of scaling operators, making that restriction explicit and providing a common basis for designing a more flexible alternative.

The proposed Single Generalized Multi-scale Architecture, or SiGMA, uses a learnable discrete Gaussian kernel grounded in scale-space theory. This kernel enables distance-aware scaling, allowing the scaling operation to be learned. The approach connects the handling of multiple temporal resolutions to one operator framework, rather than treating scaling choices as unrelated architectural components.

On the reported long- and short-term forecasting benchmarks, SiGMA outperforms the compared multi-scale methods, including best performance in 13 of 16 long-term settings. It also achieves training speed improvements of up to 5.3 times and memory reductions of up to 3.8 times over the strongest competitors. These are reported maximum gains, showing that flexible scaling can improve efficiency alongside forecasting accuracy.
icml-2026-generalizing-multi-scale-time-.tldr: SiGMA learns a distance-aware scaling operator that improves forecasting accuracy and achieves substantial training and memory savings in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Hyper-relational knowledge graphs represent facts with multiple connected components. Standard link prediction typically assumes almost all of a fact is already known and asks the model to fill one blank. This paper broadens that setting to fact generation, where any number of components may be missing, including every component.

The proposed method, KREPE, learns distributions over missing components through masked discrete diffusion. Its predictions use both the available pieces of the current fact and the surrounding graph structure. Contextual message passing models dependencies within a fact, while aggregation of randomly sampled contexts captures relationships between facts. These two sources of information help the model handle incomplete queries with different amounts of observed evidence.

KREPE trains link prediction and fact generation within one framework. The authors report state-of-the-art results on standard hyper-relational link prediction benchmarks and better generation of novel, correct facts than the compared language-model baselines. The contribution therefore extends the range of questions a knowledge-graph model can answer while also improving performance on the conventional single-blank task.
icml-2026-generative-representation-lear.tldr: KREPE uses masked discrete diffusion to complete arbitrarily missing fact components or generate whole facts in hyper-relational knowledge graphs.

paragraphs: A tabular classifier can be misled when the frequency of classes in its training context differs from the frequency encountered at prediction time. This paper finds that TabPFN is vulnerable to this label shift, often favoring the majority class in the training dataset. Strong general tabular performance therefore does not prevent sensitivity to the context’s class balance.

DistPFN addresses the problem by adjusting predicted class probabilities at test time. It reduces the influence of the training prior, meaning the class frequencies in the supplied context, and emphasizes the model’s predicted posterior. The adjustment requires neither architectural changes nor additional training. A second version, DistPFN-T, uses temperature scaling to adapt the adjustment strength according to the discrepancy between prior and posterior.

Evaluations on more than 250 OpenML datasets show substantial classification improvements under label shift across several TabPFN-based models. The methods also maintain strong performance in settings without label shift. The results support probability adjustment as a lightweight way to reduce excessive dependence on the class distribution of the training context.
icml-2026-mitigating-label-shift-in-tabu.tldr: DistPFN adjusts TabPFN’s class probabilities at test time to improve robustness to label shift without retraining.

paragraphs: Planning data collection requires estimating how a model’s performance will change as more data becomes available. A fixed mathematical curve can be a poor fit when its shape is uncertain. Gaussian processes offer greater flexibility, but existing ways of making their curves monotonic can complicate inference or require observations of derivatives.

MOVE introduces a monotonic variational Gaussian process that uses virtual-derivative factors to keep posterior inference tractable. These factors incorporate information about the direction of change into the model. The method pairs this learning-curve formulation with an expected-shortfall objective for collecting data toward a target, connecting uncertainty about future performance to the data-collection decision.

The theoretical analysis shows that expected shortfall supplies non-vanishing gradient signals, supporting reliable gradient-based optimization of that objective. Experiments on classification, segmentation, and detection benchmarks show consistent improvements over the prior method. Together, the modeling and decision components address both parts of the problem: estimating a flexible monotonic learning curve and using it to guide target-driven data collection.
icml-2026-monotonic-variational-gaussian.tldr: MOVE combines tractable monotonic Gaussian-process modeling with an expected-shortfall objective to guide data collection toward a performance target.

paragraphs: Videos can supply supervision for robot models even when the underlying actions are unavailable as labels. A latent action is a learned representation used as a substitute label, but it is useful only if it carries information about what actually happened. Viewpoint-specific visual changes can interfere with that goal by contributing information unrelated to the underlying action.

MVP-LAM learns these representations from videos with multiple viewpoints. Its training objective requires a latent action extracted from one view to explain the future in another view. Because the representation must work across cameras, the objective reduces reliance on cues specific to a single viewpoint and encourages information that describes the action itself.

On Bridge V2, the learned representations have higher mutual information with ground-truth actions and support improved action prediction, including out-of-distribution evaluation. Pretraining vision-language-action models with these latent actions also improves downstream manipulation across several benchmarks. The findings connect a more action-informative representation to better supervision for learning robot behavior.
icml-2026-mvp-lam-learning-action-centri.tldr: MVP-LAM learns latent actions across camera views, improving their connection to actual actions and their usefulness for robot pretraining.

paragraphs: Language models trained through self-play can improve initially and then lose performance as training continues. This paper analyzes that pattern as degeneration across iterations: the system generating training tasks increasingly concentrates on familiar problems. As the task distribution narrows, the learning signal becomes less useful and training becomes less stable.

The proposed approach adds a one-class novelty reward to an existing self-play pipeline. A Seen Detector learns from a historical buffer of previously used problems and identifies new candidates that fall within that familiar distribution. The reward discourages the question-generating model from repeatedly producing such problems, directing exploration toward less explored regions that remain learnable.

Experiments show that this addition mitigates iteration-collapse and produces consistent improvements during iterative training. The intervention acts on which problems the system generates, making the evolving training distribution an explicit part of stabilization. Its stated benefit is reducing the observed collapse rather than guaranteeing that every self-play process will improve indefinitely.
icml-2026-ocnr-stabilizing-self-play-by-.tldr: OCNR rewards less familiar training problems to reduce task-distribution narrowing and mitigate performance collapse during language-model self-play.

paragraphs: In multinomial logit bandits, an agent presents a subset of items and observes a single choice. Designing informative experiments is difficult because the number of possible subsets grows combinatorially. This paper seeks experiments that are statistically informative while remaining computationally feasible, avoiding direct optimization over every possible assortment.

The framework offers two complementary approaches. One reformulates the design oracle as a binary mixed-integer linear program, allowing exact solutions or certified approximations with solver-certified early stopping. The other replaces the nonlinear design objective with a tractable surrogate and runs in fully polynomial time. Using the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence theorem, the authors establish near G-optimality guarantees and describe the resulting trade-offs between information quality and computational cost.

The framework also supports an algorithm for identifying the best assortment when utilities are linear and revenues differ across items. Its proved instance-dependent sample complexity scales as d log N divided by the squared minimum revenue gap, up to suppressed logarithmic factors. This connects experimental design to the number of observations needed to distinguish the best assortment.
icml-2026-optimal-design-for-multinomial.tldr: The paper develops scalable experimental designs for multinomial logit bandits and proves sample-complexity guarantees for identifying the best assortment.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a hand interacting with a flexible object requires explaining both the hand’s motion and the object’s changing shape. Existing approaches often focus on rigid or partly rigid objects, or reconstruct deformable objects without recovering the complete hand in three dimensions. PhysHanDI addresses the joint reconstruction of interacting hands and highly deformable objects.

The framework uses densely reconstructed three-dimensional hand motion to induce forces that drive a physical simulation of object deformation. This ties the object’s dynamics to the movements of the hand and supports physically plausible reconstructions. The object is therefore modeled as responding to the interaction, with its deformation linked directly to the reconstructed hand motion.

The relationship also works in reverse: simulated object deformations provide information that can refine hand reconstruction through inverse physics. Experiments report better reconstruction and future prediction than the state-of-the-art baseline. The findings support treating hand and object estimation as a coupled physical problem, where each reconstruction can help constrain and improve the other.
icml-2026-physhandi-physics-based-recons.tldr: PhysHanDI couples hand reconstruction with physical deformation simulation to improve reconstruction and prediction of hand–deformable-object interactions.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer energy-efficient computation on neuromorphic hardware, but hardware faults can seriously reduce their performance. Existing robustness methods often need access to internal circuits to change weights or inspect network states. This paper develops a mechanism that operates entirely by controlling the input data, addressing situations where that internal access is unavailable.

The approach starts from a mismatch: faults reduce the network’s usable learning capacity, while incoming samples can still impose the original instantaneous load. It divides each sample into fragments to redistribute that load. A learnable fragmentation strategy determines both where the divisions occur and how many fragments to use, adapting the input organization to the degraded network dynamics.

Experiments show consistent improvements over previous methods across various spiking-network models without direct circuit access. The authors also demonstrate effectiveness on a physical FPGA implementation. These results support input fragmentation as a practical route to fault tolerance when modifying or monitoring the network’s internal hardware is not part of the available interface.
icml-2026-practical-mechanism-for-fault-.tldr: Learned input fragmentation improves spiking-network fault tolerance without accessing internal circuits, including on a physical FPGA platform.

paragraphs: Shapley values assign credit to contributors such as training examples or input features. Their standard treatment of contributors as interchangeable can be unsuitable when contributions depend on earlier ones or deserve different priorities. Reused data, augmented examples, causal feature orderings, and trust-related adjustments motivate a valuation rule that represents those distinctions explicitly.

Priority-Aware Shapley Value incorporates two forms of structure: hard constraints on which contributors must precede others, and soft priority weights for individual contributors. It supports general precedence structures and includes precedence-only and weight-only variants as special cases. The authors also characterize the rule uniquely through axioms, specifying the principles that determine its allocation.

For scalable estimation, the paper develops a Metropolis–Hastings sampler based on adjacent swaps and analyzes what happens under extreme priority weights. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR10, and Census Income show allocations that better reflect the specified structure. A procedure called priority sweeping exposes how allocations respond to changing priorities, making those choices available for practical sensitivity analysis.
icml-2026-priority-aware-shapley-value-c.tldr: Priority-Aware Shapley Value combines precedence constraints and contributor-specific weights to make attribution reflect dependencies and priorities.

paragraphs: This paper develops a mathematical account of agency within neural models. It represents agents as probability distributions over outcomes and evaluates their epistemic utility using a logarithmic score. The central question is how such agents can combine into a larger entity while strictly improving every constituent’s welfare under that formal definition.

The framework uses weighted logarithmic pooling to define compositions. The authors prove that strict unanimous improvement is impossible with linear pooling or with only two possible outcomes, but possible with three or more outcomes. Cloning invariance, continuity, and openness support recursive compositions, while a tilt-based analysis excludes trivial duplication. These results identify structural conditions relevant to the proposed theory of collective agency.

The authors then formalize an alignment phenomenon involving benevolent and antagonistic language-model personas, called Luigi and Waluigi. Within their theory, eliciting the benevolent persona induces an antagonistic counterpart, and manifesting then suppressing that counterpart gives a strictly greater first-order reduction in misalignment than reinforcing Luigi alone. This is a theoretical comparison within the framework.
icml-2026-probabilistic-modeling-of-late.tldr: The paper models agents as outcome distributions, characterizes mutually beneficial composition, and derives a theoretical comparison of persona-based alignment strategies.

paragraphs: Robust reinforcement learning seeks policies that perform well against adverse environmental conditions. Its optimization contains an inner search for the worst case within an uncertainty set. Exhaustively querying that set costs an amount proportional to its size, which can make robust learning expensive even before accounting for the outer policy-learning process.

Quantum Robust Inner Minimization, or QRIM, addresses this search under the assumption that the environment can be queried in quantum superposition. It encodes the uncertainty set as a superposition and amplifies cases with low returns. This supplies the worst-case component needed for the robust Bellman equation while leaving the outer reinforcement learning pipeline unchanged.

The stated query complexity improves from linear in the uncertainty-set size to its square root, a quadratic speed-up in queries. Validation spans classical simulations and execution on real quantum hardware, with more robust learned policies and quadratically fewer queries than classical reinforcement learning. The speed-up concerns query complexity under the quantum-access assumption; it is not a claim about every component of end-to-end runtime.
icml-2026-quantum-robust-inner-minimizat.tldr: Given quantum-superposition access to the environment, QRIM quadratically reduces the queries needed for robust reinforcement learning’s worst-case search.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning fine-tuning needs to improve a language model while controlling how far each policy update moves. GRPO-style methods commonly approximate this control with importance-ratio clipping and group-wise normalization. This paper identifies brittle behavior when those mechanisms fail to regulate samples whose ratios lie outside the clipping interval.

QUATRO directly enforces query-adaptive trust-region constraints through a principled optimization formulation. The resulting objective makes control over policy changes explicit and includes stabilizing terms that arise from the exact trust-region formulation itself. It also supports control of entropy, the measure of uncertainty in the model’s output distribution, throughout optimization.

Experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks show stable training with more stale policies and aggressive learning rates. Entropy remains well controlled in those evaluations. These findings matter because both delayed policy information and large updates can challenge optimization stability. The reported contribution is a more directly constrained update rule with empirical stability under those training conditions.
icml-2026-quatro-query-adaptive-trust-re.tldr: QUATRO directly constrains language-model policy updates and demonstrates stable, entropy-controlled fine-tuning under aggressive learning rates and increased policy staleness.

paragraphs: Sampling from a distribution becomes harder when samples must remain within a bounded region. Reflective Hamiltonian Monte Carlo handles boundaries through reflections, but its existing treatment relies on convex support assumptions and lacks finite-time convergence guarantees. This paper introduces a convex-container and thinning framework applicable to arbitrary target densities with bounded support.

The authors establish non-asymptotic mixing-time bounds, quantifying how long sampling takes to approach the target distribution in total variation. For targets satisfying an L-smoothness condition, the bound has quadratic dependence on dimension, O(d²), but exponential dependence on smoothness parameters. Adding an m-strong convexity assumption yields a sharper bound that removes that exponential dependence.

The framework is also applied to sampling on the Stiefel manifold through a well-conditioned polar reparameterization. Simulation studies show improved numerical stability and sampling efficiency. The theoretical and numerical contributions address complementary concerns: when the sampler can be guaranteed to approach its target, and how a suitable representation can improve its practical behavior on a constrained sampling problem.
icml-2026-reflective-hamiltonian-monte-c.tldr: The paper extends reflective HMC with finite-time mixing guarantees and improves simulated Stiefel-manifold sampling through polar reparameterization.

paragraphs: Reasoning models incur substantial inference and memory costs from long reasoning traces and growing key-value caches. Four-bit floating-point formats can reduce those costs, but quantizing weights, activations, and caches together can damage reasoning. This paper locates failures particularly at low-entropy decisions, such as selecting a digit or operator, where small errors can propagate through subsequent reasoning.

ReQAT combines three training components around that diagnosis. Trace-Aligned QAT revisits identical reasoning traces to focus updates on critical decisions. Selective Entropy Minimization reinforces confidence at low-entropy positions. Q-FIT supplies a quantization-friendly initialization that jointly calibrates key-value cache transformations consistent with rotary positional embeddings, helping stabilize quantization-aware training.

Under the same training budget, ReQAT surpasses the accuracy of BF16 fine-tuning in the reported evaluation while using the fully quantized four-bit configuration. It also delivers throughput speed-ups of up to 3.9 times on NVIDIA DGX Spark and 3.1 times on B200. The results connect protection of precise symbolic choices to both retained reasoning accuracy and faster deployment.
icml-2026-reqat-achieving-full-precision.tldr: ReQAT targets fragile symbolic decisions during four-bit training, surpassing BF16 fine-tuning accuracy under the same training budget in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Large convolution kernels can capture broad spatial context in high-resolution three-dimensional volumes, offering an alternative to vision transformers. Simply enlarging the kernels, however, can destabilize optimization. This paper investigates that problem through effective receptive fields, focusing on how different spatial positions influence learning rather than treating every kernel location identically.

The theoretical analysis shows that structurally reparameterized blocks induce spatially varying learning rates that are crucial for convergence. Rep3D turns this insight into a lightweight modulation network that generates scaling masks for kernel updates. These masks adaptively reweight learning across spatial positions according to receptive-field bias, while the main model retains a plain encoder architecture.

The framework aims to support stable learning from local to global structure without the complexity of multi-branch designs. Across five three-dimensional segmentation benchmarks, Rep3D consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art transformer and fixed-prior baselines. The findings indicate that adapting where and how strongly a large kernel learns can improve its usefulness for volumetric segmentation.
icml-2026-spatially-adaptive-gradient-re.tldr: Rep3D adaptively scales updates across large 3D convolution kernels, improving optimization and segmentation performance on five benchmarks.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can spend much of their computation and memory processing visual tokens. Removing tokens improves efficiency, but keeping only important-looking tokens can lose diversity, while prioritizing diversity can underrepresent important regions. SPLIT addresses both requirements by combining importance estimation, regional allocation, and selection of distinctive representations.

The method estimates importance from changes in hidden states across layers, avoiding attention-score-based importance estimates. It assigns adaptive token budgets to regions to preserve local coverage, then selects tokens using a diversity score that favors nonredundant information. The analysis establishes tighter coverage guarantees for adaptive budgets than uniform allocation and supports diversity preservation without costly tuning.

Experiments show consistent improvements over the compared methods on image and video understanding. With LLaVA-1.5-7B, SPLIT preserves over 99% of accuracy using 192 visual tokens and about 92.8% using 64. These results show substantial accuracy retention under tight token budgets, while also making clear that the more aggressive reduction retains a smaller share of the original performance.
icml-2026-split-vlm-salience-guided-part.tldr: SPLIT reduces visual tokens by combining importance, local coverage, and diversity, retaining substantial accuracy even under severe token budgets.

paragraphs: Continuous actor-critic policies can produce rapid, erratic changes in actions that make physical deployment difficult. Common remedies penalize roughness directly in the policy’s output. This paper instead examines the critic, whose Q-function evaluates actions and supplies the learning signal that shapes the policy.

Using implicit differentiation, the authors bound the sensitivity of the optimal policy by a ratio involving two properties of the Q-function. The numerator captures mixed-derivative sensitivity, described as sensitivity to noise, while the denominator captures curvature over actions, or how distinctly the critic favors actions. This links policy smoothness to the geometry of the critic’s learning signal.

PAVE applies that insight by treating the critic as a scalar field and stabilizing the action gradients it induces. It minimizes gradient volatility while preserving local curvature, leaving the actor unchanged. Experiments achieve smoothness comparable to methods that regularize the policy directly while maintaining competitive task performance. The results support critic regularization as an effective route to smoother control.
icml-2026-stabilizing-the-q-gradient-fie.tldr: PAVE smooths actor-critic policies by stabilizing the critic’s action gradients while preserving curvature and leaving the actor unchanged.

paragraphs: Ordinal labels express ordered categories, but a noisy annotation need not mean that one definite label was simply corrupted. An instance may reasonably correspond to several ranks. This paper makes that uncertainty central to rank estimation by treating each instance as having multiple plausible ranks and framing learning as a stochastic ordering problem.

Stochastic Order Learning, or SOL, learns an embedding space with two complementary objectives. A discriminative loss structures the relationships between instances and centroids, providing organization in the representation. A stochastic order loss enforces probabilistic ordering relationships between instances, allowing the ordering objective to account for uncertain ranks rather than requiring a single deterministic label for every example.

Experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate reliable rank estimation under different kinds and levels of label noise. The contribution is a representation-learning framework that brings label uncertainty and ordered relationships into the same training process. Its findings support modeling the structure of ordinal ambiguity directly when learning to estimate ranks from noisy annotations.
icml-2026-stochastic-order-learning-an-a.tldr: SOL models noisy ordinal labels as multiple plausible ranks and learns representations that preserve probabilistic ordering relationships.

paragraphs: The environment used to train and evaluate cooperative agents shapes which behaviors and difficulties researchers can study. Existing multi-agent benchmarks expose important challenges, but limited modularity can make custom scenarios hard to construct. TABX provides a reconfigurable battle sandbox intended to make those experimental choices more accessible.

The simulator gives researchers fine-grained control over environmental parameters. This supports systematic investigation of emerging agent behavior and algorithmic trade-offs across tasks with different levels of complexity. Its implementation uses JAX and GPU acceleration to run many simulations in parallel, reducing the computational overhead associated with collecting experience from multi-agent environments.

The paper’s contribution is a fast, extensible research environment rather than a new agent-learning algorithm. Its stated value combines customization with throughput: researchers can vary task conditions while retaining the ability to run large numbers of simulations. That combination provides a scalable basis for studying cooperative learning in complex, structured domains and for constructing evaluations around specific research questions.
icml-2026-tabx-a-high-throughput-sandbox.tldr: TABX is a customizable, GPU-accelerated battle simulator designed for high-throughput cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning research.

paragraphs: Image reconstruction is especially challenging when training data contains separate collections of noisy measurements and clean images, with no matching pairs. UOTIP learns to map between those two distributions using unbalanced optimal transport. A likelihood-based cost connects the mapping to the measurement process, making reconstruction part of the distribution-matching formulation.

The unbalanced formulation relaxes the requirement to match the distributions’ marginals exactly. The authors identify this flexibility as providing robustness to multiple observation-noise levels, adaptation to different class proportions in the noisy and clean datasets, and generalization across noise types. These properties address mismatches that can occur when the two training collections are independently assembled.

The paper also proves that adding a quadratic cost term satisfies a twist condition that ensures existence and uniqueness of the transport map, even for ill-posed inverse problems. This guarantee concerns the learned transport formulation. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on unpaired image inverse-problem benchmarks covering both linear and nonlinear problems, supporting the approach across different measurement relationships.
icml-2026-uotip-unbalanced-optimal-trans.tldr: UOTIP uses unbalanced optimal transport to learn image reconstruction from unpaired noisy and clean datasets while accommodating distribution mismatches.

paragraphs: A pretrained graph model may encounter new datasets whose node features differ in both meaning and dimensionality. Those differences make inference without retraining difficult. This paper identifies a representation axis induced by graph structure, called view space, that provides a shared basis for handling graphs with heterogeneous numerical features.

The framework introduces Graph View Transformation, a family of parametric mappings that can be shared across arbitrary graphs. Its concrete architecture, Recurrent GVT, learns node representations for fully inductive node classification. The central idea is to use structure-induced representations to bridge datasets whose raw feature spaces do not already align.

Pretrained on OGBN-Arxiv and evaluated on 27 benchmarks, Recurrent GVT outperforms GraphAny by a reported 8.93% and exceeds 12 individually tuned graph neural networks by at least 3.30%. These findings support view space as a practical basis for transfer across heterogeneous graphs. They demonstrate that a shared pretrained representation can perform strongly on unseen graph datasets without dataset-specific retraining.
icml-2026-view-space-learning-representa.tldr: Recurrent GVT uses graph-induced view-space representations to transfer a pretrained node-classification model across datasets with different feature spaces.
